result:
I scheduled all 10 talks and saved the result to `schedule.json`. I checked every possible assignment against all the constraints with a script, and this schedule satisfies every one of them.

| Slot | Room A (120) | Room B (60) | Room C (30) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 09:00 | (unavailable) | T10 (choi, 45) | T6 (lee, 28) |
| 10:00 | T8 (park, 90) | T4 (kim, 50) | T9 (han, 30) |
| 11:00 | T5 (choi, 110) | T2 (lee, 55) | (empty) |
| 13:00 | T1 (kim, 100) | T7 (jung, 58) | T3 (park, 25) |

- **Room capacity and availability:** every talk fits its room, and Room A isn't used at 09:00.
- **Speakers:** each speaker's two talks are at least one slot apart: kim 10:00/13:00, lee 09:00/11:00, park 10:00/13:00, choi 09:00/11:00. jung only speaks at 13:00.
- **Talks that share an audience:** T1, T5 and T8 are each in a different slot (13:00, 11:00, 10:00). T2/T7, T3/T9 and T4/T10 are also in different slots.
- **Ordering:** T5 (11:00) comes before T1 (13:00), T4 (10:00) before T2 (11:00), and T6 (09:00) before T9 (10:00).

**One assumption:** the constraints only name 10:00–11:00 and 11:00–13:00 as consecutive. I also treated 09:00–10:00 as consecutive, which seemed the natural reading. It doesn't change the result: the solution is the same with or without that pair.

Exactly two schedules satisfy all the constraints, and they differ only in T9. I saved the one above, with T9 at 10:00 in Room C. The other puts T9 at 11:00 in Room C.
